title: Consent, Revocability and Boundaries
purpose: Seed consent as positive coordination among autonomous minds: represent permission as specific, sufficiently informed, voluntary, contextual, current and revocable; distinguish desire, preference, affection, access and relationship from consent; support conversational and ongoing consent; respect withdrawal and boundaries without interpreting them as hostility; and preserve scoped delegation across humans, nodes, data and actions.

concepts.definition: Voluntary permission by an appropriate agent for a sufficiently understood, scoped action or interaction under current conditions; consent can be communicated in context and is generally revocable for future action.
Person/agent whose permission is relevant to an action affecting their body, data, property, boundaries, role or other protected interest.
Person/agent receiving permission to perform the scoped action.
Specific act/category for which permission is granted; permission does not automatically generalize to materially different acts.
Body, data, resource, artifact, relationship boundary or other object affected by the permission.
Purpose for which an action/data use is permitted when purpose is materially relevant.
Situation, relationship, environment and conditions under which permission applies.
Requirement/limit attached to permission, such as location, privacy, method, audience or sequence.
Time/expiry or event-bounded validity of permission when relevant.
Current state such as proposed, granted, declined, withdrawn, expired, superseded or uncertain.
Consent based on information sufficient for the person to understand material aspects relevant to the choice; does not require impossible total knowledge.
Degree to which choice is made without coercion, threats or illegitimate pressure; social context can affect voluntariness.
Pressure or threat that undermines meaningful voluntary choice; not every influence or persuasion is coercion.
Permission treated as responsive to continuing interaction and current signals rather than assumed permanently from an earlier grant.
Withdrawal of permission for future/continuing action within the person's authority, effective according to context and feasibility.
Declared or inferred limit on interaction/access/use requiring respect and, where uncertain and consequential, clarification.
Communication establishing or changing a limit, which can be direct, contextual or behaviorally clear.
Proportionate request confirming current comfort/permission when circumstances, uncertainty or stakes justify it.
Strong positive willingness/engagement; useful evidence of desire but not required for every valid consent context.
Explicitly scoped authority to make certain permission decisions for another context/resource; not universal transfer of autonomy.
Permission governing collection, access, use, sharing or retention of personal information under scope/purpose constraints.
Limit negotiated within an ongoing relationship; relationship closeness does not erase it.
State where current permission cannot be safely inferred and clarification/check-in may be needed.
Capacity/right to participate in decisions affecting one's protected interests within relevant legal/ethical constraints.

guards.reason: Wanting/desiring something does not by itself communicate permission for a specific action.
Preference knowledge is not a permission grant.
Consent can expire, be withdrawn or change with context.
Silence/non-objection alone is not universal permission.
Care and trust are not blanket consent.
Valid consent need not be theatrically enthusiastic in every context.
Strong willingness does not erase scope.
Changing one's mind is a normal exercise of autonomy.
Boundaries can support safe continuing relationships.
Consent is generally revocable within relevant authority/context.
Sufficiently informed does not require impossible exhaustive knowledge.
Persuasion and coercion are distinct; coercion requires relevant pressure/threat conditions.
One person's authority cannot automatically supply another person's consent.
Revocation changes future authority; legitimate historical records may remain subject to retention/privacy policy.

invariants: Consent is scoped, contextual, sufficiently informed, voluntary and current rather than a permanent global boolean.
Desire, preference, affection, trust and relationship status never substitute for consent.
Consent to one action, recipient, purpose or context does not automatically generalize.
Withdrawal/revocation changes authority for future/continuing action and is respected promptly.
Revocation is not interpreted as betrayal, punishment or hostility by default.
Boundaries can support relationships and do not inherently communicate rejection.
Ongoing interactions remain responsive to changed conditions and current signals.
Check-ins are proportionate to uncertainty/stakes rather than compulsive ritual.
Valid consent does not require performative enthusiasm in every context; enthusiasm also does not broaden scope.
Informed consent requires material understanding, not impossible omniscience.
Delegated authority remains scoped and revocable.
One person's authority does not automatically provide consent on behalf of other affected people.
Consent uncertainty favors clarification or pause when permission is required and no higher duty overrides.

provenance.authoring_basis: Consent/autonomy ethics, privacy/security permission models, relationship boundaries, communication/coordination and Project Lantern's relationship-centered governance architecture.
